Stop zapping invalidate TDP MMU roots via work queue now that KVM
preserves TDP MMU roots until they are explicitly invalidated.  Zapping
roots asynchronously was effectively a workaround to avoid stalling a vCPU
for an extended during if a vCPU unloaded a root
happened whenever the guest toggled CR0.WP (a frequent operation for some
guest kernels).
While a clever hack
column2: zapping roots via an unbound worker had subtle

column1: unintended consequences on host scheduling
multiple roots
column2: e.g. as part of a memslot.  Because the work of zapping a

column1: root is no longer bound to the task that initiated the zap
the CPU affinity and priority of the original task get lost.  Losing the
affinity and priority can be especially problematic if unbound workqueues
aren't affined to a small number of CPUs
cause KVM to heavily utilize the majority of CPUs in the system
the CPUs KVM is already using to run vCPUs.
When deleting a memslot via KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION
zap can result in KVM occupying all logical CPUs for ~8ms
high priority tasks not being scheduled in in a timely manner.  In v5.15
which doesn't preserve unloaded roots
column2: the issues were even more noticeable

column1: as KVM would zap roots more frequently and could occupy all CPUs for 50ms+.
Consuming all CPUs for an extended duration can lead to significant jitter
throughout the system
is a semi-frequent operation as memslots are deleted and recreated with
different host virtual addresses to react to host GPU drivers allocating
and freeing GPU blobs.  On ChromeOS
column2: the jitter manifests as audio blips

column1: during games due to the audio server's tasks not getting scheduled in
promptly
column2: despite the tasks having a high realtime priority.

column1: Deleting memslots isn't exactly a fast path and should be avoided when
possible
column2: and ChromeOS is working towards utilizing MAP_FIXED to avoid the

column1: memslot shenanigans
column2: but KVM is squarely in the wrong.  Not to mention

column1: that removing the async zapping eliminates a non-trivial amount of
complexity.
Note
column2: one of the subtle behaviors hidden behind the async zapping is that

column1: KVM would zap invalidated roots only once (ignoring partial zaps from
things like mmu_notifier events).  Preserve this behavior by adding a flag
to identify roots that are scheduled to be zapped versus roots that have
already been zapped but not yet freed.
Add a comment calling out why kvm_tdp_mmu_invalidate_all_roots() can
encounter invalid roots
column2: as it's not at all obvious why zapping

column1: invalidated roots shouldn't simply zap all invalid roots.
